Empêchée d’entrer au Canada, Rima Hassan: Barred From Entering Canada, Rima Hassan Mobilizes Montréal Remotely: An Evening Devoted to Antifascist Convergence
Conférence à Montréal: Rima Hassan, via: Conference in Montréal: Rima Hassan, by video link, and the Résistances panel call for united struggles and denounce Gaza and the far right.
À l’écran, Rima Hassan s’adresse au publ: On screen, Rima Hassan addresses the audience gathered in Montréal, taking part remotely in an evening of antifascist convergence. Photo credit: André Querry.
La Converse a assisté à la conférence «: La Converse attended the conference “Résistances contre l’extrême droite et le fascisme” (Resistance Against the Far Right and Fascism), held on March 31, to closely document this antifascist activist current, its discourse, its dynamics and its roots in Montréal, amid a rise in identitarian right-wing movements here and abroad.
Au moment de la rédaction de ce texte, l: As this article was being written, MEP Rima Hassan, whose remarks are widely reported here, was taken into police custody in France in a separate case involving accusations of condoning terrorism. She has since been released, and a hearing is scheduled for a later date. The political party La France Insoumise (LFI) denounced irregularities in the proceedings, notably the circumvention of the parliamentary immunity Rima Hassan enjoys, and the orchestrated leaking of investigation materials to right-wing media.
Cette mésaventure est survenue après l’é: This ordeal occurred after the event covered here and is not related to her participation in the Montréal conference, but it is mentioned to clarify the context in which this article is published.
<strong>Empêchée de se rendre à Montréal: Prevented from travelling to Montréal, MEP Rima Hassan spoke by video link to nearly a thousand people gathered at the Salle Pierre-Mercure on March 31. Amid denunciations of the rise of the far right, criticism of the shortcomings of international law and the centrality of the Palestinian cause, the speakers called for a convergence of struggles, in a context marked by geopolitical tensions and debates over the positioning of the left in Quebec.
Ce soir-là, près d’un millier de personn: That evening, nearly a thousand people fill the Salle Pierre-Mercure at the Université du Québec à Montréal. It is a diverse crowd, with many young people and students, attentive and responsive. Outside, in the lobby, the mobilization begins even before people enter the hall. Booths line the walls: the Ripostes collective, the UQAM student union and Palestine solidarity groups are all there. Activists from Alternatives hand out their newspaper for free, the<l1> Global Sumud Flotilla</l1> collective collects donations for a humanitarian flotilla leaving for Gaza in a few days, and Amnesty International seeks signatures <l2>against GardaWorld’s collaboration with ICE</l2>, the U.S. immigration services.
À l’intérieur, les interventions sont po: Inside, the speeches are punctuated by applause, sometimes laughter. From afar, French-Palestinian Rima Hassan speaks several times. Born in a refugee camp in Syria, she is now a member of the European Parliament for the left-wing party La France Insoumise. For nearly three hours, she addresses the audience and trades remarks with the panel members, very often adjusting her keffiyeh, which she has chosen to wear over one shoulder. Despite the distance imposed by the screen, the audience responds with enthusiasm and warmth to her analyses and her jokes.
Mais tout s’inverse au moment où l’insou: But the mood shifts when the France Insoumise MEP drops the light tone and says, with a tremor in her voice that she struggles to hide: “It’s too late for the Palestinians.” In the hall, stupefaction turns to silence at these emotionally charged words. She qualifies her remarks, however, immediately refocusing the idea on<l1> the Gaza Strip, 90 per cent of which has been destroyed</l1>, she says. Far from resignation, she immediately shifts the burden of responsibility: “It is precisely up to states […] to take stock of their policies,” calling on governments to “ask for forgiveness” and warning of what comes next: “The next territory is the West Bank.” In the same breath, she criticizes a “complacent […] left,” framing her remarks as political confrontation rather than surrender.
Faute de visa, c’est à travers son télép: Without a visa, Rima Hassan speaks through her cell phone. Her electronic travel authorization (eTA), which had initially been approved, was subject to a last-minute review. “The reasons given are the absence of any mention of a visa or entry refusal by a country (Israel), as well as the absence of any mention of an alleged criminal offence, arrest, indictment or conviction,” she said in a social media post.
D’emblée, elle décrit une « situation ka: Right away, she describes a “Kafkaesque situation.” Having arrived at the airport to catch her flight to Montréal, she was told by border police that she first had to produce a number of documents: proof of all her professional experience over the past 10 years, all her bank statements for the past two years, all proof of residence for the past 10 years, and so on. She also had to fill out a family file, provide evidence and court documents, and supply a copy of her criminal record. “Clearly, it was impossible for me to produce them in half an hour, an hour before the boarding gate closed.” She is blunt: “It was really done […] to make it impossible for me to travel”; then she denounces “a matter of censorship or intimidation.”
Interrogé en marge de l’événement, Amir: Interviewed on the sidelines of the event, Amir Khadir, a former Québec solidaire MNA, directly links Rima Hassan’s being barred to a broader political climate. “It’s distressing to see that Canada continues to repress any independent voice on Palestine,” he says, placing the episode within a dynamic he considers systemic. He denounces a contradiction between the federal government’s words and its practices: “The Canadian government puffs out its chest to pretend it’s independent from the United States, and goes off to give fine speeches at Davos. In reality, it’s the same absolutely despicable routine.” According to him, this continuity translates into a lack of concrete measures: “Doing nothing concrete against Israel […] doing nothing concrete to distance itself from the actions taken by the United States.”
Il lie aussi cet empêchement à des press: He also links her being barred to internal political pressure: “Everyone laments the Israeli lobby’s ability to dictate how things are done.” Canadian Jewish organizations celebrated on their social media that the guest had been prevented from entering Canada. B’nai Brith even claimed that the decision by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) was made on the basis of information it had provided.
Contacté par <em>La Converse</em>, le mi: Contacted by La Converse, Canada’s Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship says it cannot “comment on individual cases” because of privacy laws. In a written response, the department nonetheless specifies that “decisions regarding the issuance of travel documents are made […] on a case-by-case basis” and that applicants must “meet the requirements set out in Canadian law.” It points out that an eTA “does not guarantee entry to Canada” and can be cancelled, notably when information is deemed incomplete or inaccurate. The department does not respond on Rima Hassan’s case, and avoids confirming or denying that it responded to requests from Jewish organizations. It stresses, however, that “a person cannot be refused entry to Canada because of their personal beliefs or political opinions,” adding that travellers can submit a new application once the grounds for refusal have been resolved.
Sur la même question, Nimâ Machouf, l’an: On the same issue, Nimâ Machouf, the conference’s moderator, denounces a “double standard” that she finds “appalling.” On the sidelines of the conference, she pointed to a direct contradiction: “The Canadian government does not authorize Rima Hassan to come, but authorizes Israeli soldiers to give classes and talks in Quebec schools [see the sidebar below].” For her, this situation calls for accountability.
Il est cependant à noter que les organis: It should be noted, however, that not all Canadian Jewish organizations have taken this position. In fact, <l1>Independent Jewish Voices (IJV) is one of the organizers of the conference</l1> in which Rima Hassan was to take part.
<strong>Convergence des luttes, Palestin: Convergence of struggles, Palestine and the crisis of international law
Dès l’ouverture de la conférence, Vaness: From the opening of the conference, Vanessa Gordon, a member of the Alternatives collective, co-organizer of the event, sets the tone: “The expansion of the far right and fascism calls for the building of a strong political movement […] that is emancipatory, decolonial, inclusive.” She ties this necessity to a historical trajectory: “More than 40 years of neoliberalism have led to social fragmentation and a widespread sense of powerlessness.”
Dans ce cadre, la Palestine devient cent: In this framework, Palestine becomes central. “We are generally stuck in the throat of the world, and no one will manage to swallow us,” says Rima Hassan, quoting Palestinian poet and diplomat Elias Sanbar on the place the Palestinian cause occupies today. Starting from this idea, she redefines the issue: “Palestine really needs to be understood as a collective liberation struggle more than as a national liberation struggle.”
Cette articulation mène à une critique d: This framing leads to a critique of international law. “The problem isn’t the law […] everything comes down to political will,” she says, denouncing the lack of action against Israel, as well as the double standard Western powers apply in resolving conflicts: “There is political will to end the crimes in Ukraine. There is no will at all for Israel.”
Le diagnostic est partagé : le droit int: The diagnosis is shared: international law is weakened, even instrumentalized. Journalist and essayist Émilie Nicolas picks up the idea, saying that international law has “blind spots,” having been designed “when very few nations were independent” and now producing a “collective dissonance.”
Le panel Résistances : Jonathan Duran Fo: The Résistances panel: Jonathan Duran Folco, Safa Chebbi, Haroun Bouazzi, Émilie Nicolas and Nima Machouf. Photo credit: André Querry.
<strong>Gaza, responsabilités occidental: Gaza, Western responsibilities and the transformation of the right
En plus d’Émilie Nicolas, l’animatrice d: Besides Émilie Nicolas, the debate’s moderator, Nimâ Machouf, leads a panel made up of Jonathan Durand Folco, essayist and university professor; Québec solidaire MNA for Maurice-Richard, Haroun Bouazzi; and Safa Chebbi, director of the Observatoire des inégalités raciales du Québec. Half the panel, namely Rima Hassan, Nimâ Machouf and Safa Chebbi, took part in the Freedom Flotilla, organized in 2025 to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza. The ships were intercepted.
Les échanges sur le droit international: The discussion of international law then turns to Gaza and the notion of complicity which, for Rima Hassan, rests on two criteria: having knowledge and providing logistical support. “These policies are made in our name,” the MEP insists, to show that the argument shifts responsibility onto citizens.
Safa Chebbi ancre ce propos dans le cont: Safa Chebbi anchors this point in the Quebec context: “There are arms companies […] in which public money is invested.” She underlines an indirect reality: “We don’t supply weapons directly, but parts that make it possible to manufacture them.” Her demonstration, backed by figures, presents a war economy woven into local economic logic through entities she names.
Parallèlement, Jonathan Durand Folco ana: Meanwhile, Jonathan Durand Folco analyzes the evolution of the right and distinguishes several strategies: “Some use the language of law to discriminate,” while others free themselves from it altogether. In Trump’s case, he argues, it’s more like: “I don’t give a damn about the rules.” He also warns of an international coordination that he says is under way. “They’re organizing among themselves,” says Mr. Durand Folco, speaking of Western regimes that are turning into “authoritarian democracies.”
Ces interventions convergent vers un mêm: These remarks converge on a single conclusion: the weakening of legal frameworks and a reshuffling of power relations on the international stage.
<strong>Une salle engagée, entre ancrage: An engaged room, between local roots and international dynamics
Plus localement, une question du public: On a more local note, a question from the audience raised a certain “timidity” on the part of the Quebec left in the face of a far right seen as on the offensive. Haroun Bouazzi counters this critical reading with a more nuanced view, rooted in local mobilizations. “Me, I’m very optimistic because there are an enormous number of courageous lefts in Quebec,” he says, citing the encampments outside the Caisse de dépôt, the massive strikes in public services and the mobilizations in the community sector. He does, however, distinguish civil society from the partisan sphere: “I won’t talk too much about the political left […] but it needs that base to become more and more courageous.”
Les témoignages recueillis dans la salle: Testimonies gathered in the room point to an attentive reception, but also one marked by worries and questions. One student, who prefers to remain anonymous, is excited “to see that there are many people fighting for the Palestinian cause,” but says she perceives “a rise of the right, of the far right […] both locally and around the world,” a development that, in her view, makes it necessary “to come together” and “think collectively” about how to respond. Another student speaks of a need for clearer political bearings, saying the evening helps her “better understand the links between what’s happening elsewhere and here,” particularly on issues of racism, colonialism and student mobilizations.
Dans les échanges, une même préoccupatio: In the conversations, the same concern keeps coming up: how do we turn these observations into concrete action? Houssam Sabouni, who came to the conference to hear Rima Hassan, puts this worry in direct terms: “If we don’t come together, if we don’t try to think of ways to counter the rise of fascisms, it’s going to come, it’s going to affect everyone.” Between a desire to get involved, a need for tools and questions about which forms of action to favour, these voices sketch the portrait of an audience looking for structure in a context perceived as increasingly unstable.
La soirée se conclut ; l’atmosphère est: The evening ends; the atmosphere is a mix of worry and mobilization. The audience’s reactions reflect strong involvement. When Haroun Bouazzi calls out “Siamo tutti…,” the room answers in chorus: “antifascisti!” The slogan, which means “We are all antifascists!”, originated in Italy in the 1920s, at the heart of the mobilizations against Benito Mussolini’s regime.

Deux jours après la conférence, Rima Has: Two days after the conference, Rima Hassan was arrested in France, then released. Her arrest had no connection to this conference, but was tied to an accusation of condoning terrorism for having shared a quote from Kozo Okamoto referring to the Palestinian cause and resistance to oppression. A member of a militant organization called the “Japanese Red Army,” Okamoto carried out a massacre at an Israeli airport in 1972.
Rima Hassan a été libérée en vue de son: Rima Hassan was released pending her hearing, which will take place on July 7. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, founder of La France Insoumise, denounced the arrest, citing parliamentary immunity. On Friday, the MEP <l1>denounced</l1> the proliferation of proceedings against her, saying she is the target of “judicial harassment” because of her political positions.
La présence de militaires israéliens dan: The presence of Israeli soldiers in two private Jewish schools in Montréal has recently sparked a political controversy in Quebec. According to an article published on February 26 in La Presse, active or former members of the Israeli army were repeatedly invited to give talks to students, sometimes as part of activities including simulated military training.
La ministre de l’Éducation, Sonia LeBel,: Education Minister Sonia LeBel called the situation “extremely concerning” and launched checks to assess the nature of these visits and their compliance with the rules governing subsidized institutions.
Sur le plan politique, plusieurs partis: On the political front, several opposition parties denounced the visits, deeming them incompatible with the role of educational institutions, particularly in a context of war in Gaza.
